question: A receiving facility identifies a hazard in a raw material controlled by its supplier. What supplier verification activities does Part 117 allow, and how is the appropriate one selected?

context.heading: General requirements applicable to a supply-chain program.

context.text:
(a) (a) Approval of suppliers. The receiving facility must approve suppliers in accordance with the requirements of § 117.410(d), and document that approval, before receiving raw materials and other ingredients received from those suppliers;
(b) (b) Written procedures for receiving raw materials and other ingredients.
context.heading: Using approved suppliers.

context.text:
(a) (a) Except as provided by paragraph (c), (d), or (e) of this section, one or more of the supplier verification activities specified in § 117.410(b), as determined under § 117.410(d), must be conducted for each supplier before using the raw material or other ingredient from that supplier and periodically thereafter.
(b)(1) (b)(1) Except as provided by paragraph (b)(2) of this section, when a hazard in a raw material or other ingredient will be controlled by the supplier and is one for which there is a reasonable probability that exposure to the hazard will result in serious adverse health consequences or death to humans:
(b)(1)(i) (i) The appropriate supplier verification activity is an onsite audit of the supplier; and
(b)(2) (2) The requirements of paragraph (b)(1) of this section do not apply if there is a written determination that other verification activities and/or less frequent onsite auditing of the supplier provide adequate assurance that the hazards are controlled.
(c) (c) If a supplier is a qualified facility as defined by § 117.3, the receiving facility does not need to comply with paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section if the receiving facility:
context.heading: Conducting supplier verification activities for raw materials and other ingredients.

answer:
The permitted activities (21 CFR 117.410(b)). The appropriate supplier verification activities for raw materials and other ingredients are onsite audits (117.410(b)(1)); sampling and testing; review of the supplier's relevant food safety records (117.410(b)(3)); and other appropriate activities based on supplier performance and the risk associated with the raw material or ingredient (117.410(b)(4)).

How the appropriate one is selected (117.410(d)(1)). In approving suppliers and determining the appropriate verification activities and the frequency with which they are conducted, you must consider the hazard analysis of the food, including the nature of the hazard controlled before receipt of the raw material or ingredient (117.410(d)(1)(i)); and the supplier's food safety history relevant to the materials you receive from it, including available information about results from testing for hazards and audit results relating to the safety of the food (117.410(d)(1)(iii)(C)), among the other listed factors. Suppliers must be approved in accordance with 117.410(d) and that approval documented before receiving materials from them (117.420(a)).

When the activity must be conducted (117.430). Except as 117.430(c), (d) or (e) provide, one or more of the activities specified in 117.410(b), as determined under 117.410(d), must be conducted for each supplier before using the raw material or ingredient and periodically thereafter.

The severe-hazard rule. Where a hazard will be controlled by the supplier and is one for which there is a reasonable probability that exposure would result in serious adverse health consequences or death, the appropriate verification activity is an onsite audit of the supplier (117.430(b)(1), (b)(1)(i)). That requirement does not apply where there is a written determination that other verification activities, or less frequent onsite auditing, provide adequate assurance that the hazards are controlled (117.430(b)(2)).

extra.key_elements: Onsite audit, sampling and testing, review of supplier food safety records; selection based on hazard severity and supplier performance; annual onsite audit for SAHCODHA hazards.
extra.baseline_failure_note: No answer delivered: validation withheld the draft. The permitted activities (onsite audit, sampling and testing, records review) and the annual onsite audit required for serious-health-consequence hazards under 117.430(b)(1) are absent.

question: A distributor returns a dietary supplement. What does Part 111 require the manufacturer to do with it?

context.text: — You must identify and quarantine returned dietary supplements until quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision.
context.heading: What requirements apply when a returned dietary supplement is received?

context.text:
— You must destroy, or otherwise suitably dispose of, any returned dietary supplement unless the outcome of a material review and disposition decision is that quality control personnel do the following:
(a) (a) Approve the salvage of the returned dietary supplement for redistribution or
(b) (b) Approve the returned dietary supplement for reprocessing.
context.heading: When must a returned dietary supplement be destroyed, or otherwise suitably disposed of?

context.text: — You may salvage a returned dietary supplement only if quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision to allow the salvage.
context.heading: When may a returned dietary supplement be salvaged?

context.text:
(a) (a) You must ensure that any returned dietary supplements that are reprocessed meet all product specifications established in accordance with § 111.70(e); and
(b) (b) Quality control personnel must approve or reject the release for distribution of any returned dietary supplement that is reprocessed.
context.heading: What requirements apply to a returned dietary supplement that quality control personnel approve for reprocessing?

answer:
Identify and quarantine first. You must identify and quarantine returned dietary supplements until quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision (21 CFR 111.510). Nothing happens to the returned product until that review is done.

The default is disposal. You must destroy, or otherwise suitably dispose of, any returned dietary supplement unless the outcome of the material review and disposition decision is that quality control personnel approve the salvage of the product for redistribution, or approve it for reprocessing (111.515(a), (b)).

Salvage. You may salvage a returned dietary supplement only if quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision to allow the salvage (111.520). There is no route to redistribution that bypasses that decision.

Reprocessing. Where quality control personnel approve reprocessing, you must ensure that any reprocessed returned dietary supplements meet all product specifications established in accordance with 111.70(e), and quality control personnel must approve or reject the release for distribution of the reprocessed product (111.525(a), (b)).

So the decision-maker at every branch is quality control personnel, and the sequence is quarantine, material review, then disposal unless salvage or reprocessing is approved.

extra.key_elements: Identify and quarantine, QC review, destruction or reprocessing conditions, salvage limits, investigation of other batches.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Gives a generic written-procedures answer cited to 111.103. The actual requirements - identify and quarantine the return until quality-control review (111.510), destroy it unless salvage or reprocessing is approved (111.515, 111.520), and meet product specifications on reprocessing (111.525) - are absent.

question: A finished batch fails an identity specification. What does Part 111 require the firm to do, and who makes the disposition decision?

context.text: — You must determine whether the specifications you establish under § 111.70 are met.
context.heading: What is your responsibility for determining whether established specifications are met?

context.text:
(a) (a) Before you use a component, you must:
(a)(1)(i) (1)(i) Conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify the identity of any component that is a dietary ingredient, unless you petition the agency under paragraph (a)(1)(ii) of this section and the agency exempts you from such testing;
(a)(2)(ii) (ii) Rely on a certificate of analysis from the supplier of the component that you receive, provided that:
(b) (b) You must monitor the in-process points, steps, or stages where control is necessary to ensure the quality of the finished batch of dietary supplement to:
(c) (c) For a subset of finished dietary supplement batches that you identify through a sound statistical sampling plan (or for every finished batch), you must verify that your finished batch of the dietary supplement meets product specifications for identity, purity, strength, composition, and for limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate or that may lead to adulteration of the finished batch of the dietary supplement. To do so:
(c)(3) (3) You must provide adequate documentation of your basis for determining that compliance with the specification(s) selected under paragraph (c)(1) of this section, through the use of appropriate tests or examinations conducted under paragraph (c)(2) of this section, will ensure that your finished batch of the dietary supplement meets all product specifications for identity, purity, strength, and composition, and the limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate, or that may lead to the adulteration of, the dietary supplement; and
(c)(4) (4) Your quality control personnel must review and approve the documentation that you provide under paragraph (c)(3) of this section.
(d)(1) (d)(1) You may exempt one or more product specifications from verification requirements in paragraph (c)(1) of this section if you determine and document that the specifications you select under paragraph (c)(1) of this section for determination of compliance with specifications are not able to verify that the production and process control system is producing a dietary supplement that meets the exempted product specification and there is no scientifically valid method for testing or examining such exempted product specification at the finished batch stage. In such a case, you must document why, for example, any component and in-process testing, examination, or monitoring, and any other information, will ensure that such exempted product specification is met without verification through periodic testing of the finished batch; and
(d)(2) (2) Your quality control personnel must review and approve the documentation that you provide under paragraph (d)(1) of this section.
context.heading: What must you do to determine whether specifications are met?

context.text: — Quality control personnel must conduct all required material reviews and make all required disposition decisions.
context.heading: Who conducts a material review and makes a disposition decision?

context.text: (a) (a) You must not reprocess a rejected dietary supplement or treat or provide an in-process adjustment to a component, packaging, or label to make it suitable for use in the manufacture of a dietary supplement unless:
context.heading: What requirements apply to treatments, in-process adjustments, and reprocessing when there is a deviation or unanticipated occurrence or when a specification established in accordance with § 111.70 is not met?

answer:
The obligation to determine. You must determine whether the specifications you establish under 21 CFR 111.70 are met (111.73). For a finished batch that includes verifying identity: you must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify the identity of any component that is a dietary ingredient, unless the agency has exempted you on petition (111.75(a)(1)(i)); and you must monitor the in-process points, steps or stages where control is necessary to determine whether in-process specifications are met (111.75(b)).

Who decides. Quality control personnel must conduct all required material reviews and make all required disposition decisions (111.87). So a failed identity specification goes to quality control personnel for material review and disposition - not to production.

What may then be done (111.90). You must not reprocess a rejected dietary supplement, or treat or make an in-process adjustment to a component, packaging or label to make it suitable for use, unless the conditions 111.90(a) sets out are satisfied. Reprocessing is therefore conditional, not a default remedy for a failed specification.

The quality control role runs through the section generally: quality control personnel must review and approve the documentation supporting supplier qualification (111.75(a)(2)(ii)(E)), the documentation under 111.75(c)(3) (111.75(c)(4)), and any documented exemption of a product specification from the verification requirements (111.75(d)(1), (d)(2)).

extra.key_elements: Determine whether specs are met, quality control personnel material review and disposition, treatment of deviations, reprocessing limits.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Correctly says quality-control personnel make the disposition decision, but that proposition (111.87) is cited to 111.103, and the firm's obligations under 111.73, 111.75 and 111.90 (determine whether specifications are met, reprocessing limits) are absent.

question: An importer learns that a foreign supplier failed to control a hazard. What does FSVP require?

context.text:
(a) (a) You must promptly take appropriate corrective actions if you determine that a foreign supplier of food you import does not produce the food in compliance with processes and procedures that provide at least the same level of public health protection as those required under section 418 or 419 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, if either is applicable, and the implementing regulations, or produces food that is adulterated under section 402 or misbranded under section 403(w) (if applicable) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. This determination could be based on a review of consumer, customer, or other complaints related to food safety, the verification activities conducted under § 1.506 or § 1.511(c), a reevaluation of the risks posed by the food and the foreign supplier's performance conducted under § 1.505(c) or (d), or any other relevant information you obtain. The appropriate corrective actions will depend on the circumstances but could include discontinuing use of the foreign supplier until the cause or causes of noncompliance, adulteration, or misbranding have been adequately addressed. You must document any corrective actions you take in accordance with this paragraph.
(b) (b) If you determine, by means other than the verification activities conducted under § 1.506 or § 1.511(c) or a reevaluation conducted under § 1.505(c) or (d), that a foreign supplier of food that you import does not produce food in compliance with processes and procedures that provide at least the same level of public health protection as those required under section 418 or 419 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, if either is applicable, and the implementing regulations, or produces food that is adulterated under section 402 or misbranded under section 403(w) (if applicable) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, you must promptly investigate to determine whether your FSVP is adequate and, when appropriate, modify your FSVP. You must document any investigations, corrective actions, and changes to your FSVP that you undertake in accordance with this paragraph.
(c) (c) This section does not limit your obligations with respect to other laws enforced by FDA, such as those relating to product recalls.
context.heading: What corrective actions must I take under my FSVP?

answer:
You must act promptly. Under 21 CFR 1.508(a), if you determine that a foreign supplier of food you import does not produce the food in compliance with processes and procedures that provide at least the same level of public health protection as those required under section 418 or 419 of the Act, or produces food that is adulterated or misbranded with respect to allergen labeling, you must promptly take appropriate corrective action. What is appropriate depends on the nature of the hazard and the supplier's non-compliance.

Where you learn of it by another route (1.508(b)). If you make that determination by means other than the verification activities conducted under 1.506 or 1.511(c), or a reevaluation under 1.505(c) or (d), you must promptly investigate to determine whether your FSVP is adequate and, when appropriate, modify it. So learning of a failure outside your planned verification is itself a trigger to test the programme, not only the supplier.

What this does not displace (1.508(c)). The section does not limit your obligations under other laws enforced by FDA, such as those relating to product recalls. Corrective action under FSVP is in addition to, not instead of, any recall or reporting duty.

So three things follow: prompt corrective action on the supplier relationship, investigation of whether the FSVP itself is adequate with modification where needed, and separate compliance with any recall obligation.

extra.key_elements: Prompt appropriate corrective action, investigation, determination whether the FSVP is adequate, and modification as necessary.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Answers with the approved-supplier procedures of 1.506 rather than the corrective-action duty. 1.508's requirements - promptly take appropriate corrective action, investigate, determine whether the programme is adequate and modify it as necessary - are absent, and one citation marker resolved to no source.

question: What must a firm do when it receives a product complaint about a dietary supplement?

context.text: — You must establish and follow written procedures to fulfill the requirements of this subpart O.
context.heading: What are the requirements under this subpart O for written procedures?

context.text:
(a) (a) A qualified person must:
(a)(1) (1) Review all product complaints to determine whether the product complaint involves a possible failure of a dietary supplement to meet any of its specifications, or any other requirements of this part 111, including those specifications and other requirements that, if not met, may result in a risk of illness or injury; and
(a)(2) (2) Investigate any product complaint that involves a possible failure of a dietary supplement to meet any of its specifications, or any other requirements of this part, including those specifications and other requirements that, if not met, may result in a risk of illness or injury.
(b) (b) Quality control personnel must review and approve decisions about whether to investigate a product complaint and review and approve the findings and followup action of any investigation performed.
(c) (c) The review and investigation of the product complaint by a qualified person, and the review by quality control personnel about whether to investigate a product complaint, and the findings and followup action of any investigation performed, must extend to all relevant batches and records.
context.heading: What requirements apply to the review and investigation of a product complaint?

answer:
Written procedures first. You must establish and follow written procedures to fulfil the requirements of subpart O (21 CFR 111.553).

Review and investigation (111.560(a)). A qualified person must review all product complaints to determine whether the complaint involves a possible failure of a dietary supplement to meet any of its specifications, or any other requirement of Part 111, including those which, if not met, may result in a risk of illness or injury (111.560(a)(1)); and must investigate any complaint that does involve such a possible failure (111.560(a)(2)).

Quality control's role (111.560(b)). Quality control personnel must review and approve the decisions about whether to investigate a product complaint, and must review and approve the findings and follow-up action of any investigation performed. So the qualified person screens and investigates; quality control personnel approve both the decision and the outcome.

Scope of the work (111.560(c)). The review and investigation by the qualified person, the quality control review of whether to investigate, and the findings and follow-up action of any investigation must extend to all relevant batches and records - not only the batch complained of.

extra.key_elements: QC personnel review, determine whether complaint involves a possible CGMP failure, investigate, record required information.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Answers with dietary-supplement labelling and retailer adverse-event reporting text drawn from an FDA guidance. The qualified-person review, the possible-CGMP-failure determination and the investigation duty (111.560) are never mentioned.

question: If ISO publishes a new edition of ISO 13485, does that new edition automatically become the standard required by Part 820?

context.text:
— Certain material is incorporated by reference into this part with the approval of the Director of the Federal Register under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51. All approved incorporation by reference (IBR) material is available for inspection at the Food and Drug Administration, and at the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Contact FDA at: Dockets Management Staff, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852; 240-402-7500; https://www.regulations.gov/document/FDA-2013-S-0610-0003. For information on the availability of this material at NARA, visit www.archives.gov/federal-register/cfr/ibr-locations or email fr.inspection@nara.gov. This material may be obtained from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), BIBC II, Chemin de Blandonnet 8, CP 401, 1214 Vernier, Geneva, Switzerland; +41-22-749-01-11; customerservice@iso.org, https://www.iso.org/store.html.
(a) (a) ISO 9000:2015(E) (“ISO 9000”), Quality Management systems—Fundamentals and vocabulary, Clause 3—Terms and definitions, Fourth edition, September 15, 2015. IBR approved for § 820.3.
(b) (b) ISO 13485:2016(E) (“ISO 13485”), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016; IBR approved for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45.
context.heading: Incorporation by reference.

answer:
No. A new edition does not automatically become the standard required by Part 820.

Incorporation by reference fixes a specific edition. 21 CFR 820.7 incorporates certain material by reference with the approval of the Director of the Federal Register under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51, and it names the editions precisely: ISO 9000:2015(E), Clause 3, Terms and definitions, Fourth edition, September 15, 2015, IBR approved for 820.3 (820.7(a)); and ISO 13485:2016(E), Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016, IBR approved for 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45 (820.7(b)).

What that means in practice. The obligation under 820.10(a) is to document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 as incorporated - that is, the 2016 third edition named in 820.7(b). A later edition published by ISO is not what the regulation points to, and it does not displace the named edition. FDA would have to amend 820.7 through rulemaking, with the Federal Register approval the section describes, for a new edition to become the incorporated standard.

So until that happens, the 2016 third edition remains the requirement, whatever edition is current at ISO.

extra.key_elements: No. Incorporation by reference fixes the 2016 third edition until FDA amends the regulation; a later edition does not apply automatically.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Answers the question backwards: 'the new edition automatically becomes the standard required by Part 820'. Incorporation by reference fixes the 2016 third edition until FDA amends the regulation, so a manufacturer following this answer would apply the wrong standard. Cited to 820.10, 820.3 and 820.45, none of which say it.

question: What controls does Part 820 require over labeling and packaging operations to prevent mixups, and what must be documented?

context.heading: Device labeling and packaging controls.

answer:
The controls. In addition to the requirements of Clause 7.5.1 of ISO 13485, Control of production and service provision, incorporated by reference at 21 CFR 820.7, each manufacturer must document and maintain procedures giving a detailed description of the activities to ensure the integrity, inspection, storage and operations for labeling and packaging during the customary conditions of processing, storage, handling and distribution (820.45).

Preventing mixups (820.45(c)). The manufacturer must ensure that labeling and packaging operations have been established and maintained to prevent mixups, including but not limited to inspection of the labeling and packaging before use to assure that all devices have correct labeling and packaging as specified in the medical device file.

What must be documented. The results of that labeling inspection must be documented in accordance with Clause 4.2.5 of ISO 13485 (820.45(c)), and the release of the labeling for use must likewise be documented in accordance with Clause 4.2.5 (820.45(b)).

What the examination must cover (820.45(a)). Labeling and packaging must be examined for accuracy prior to release or storage where applicable, including the correct unique device identifier or universal product code or other device identification, the expiration date, the storage instructions, the handling instructions and any additional processing instructions.

extra.key_elements: Labeling and packaging operations must be controlled to prevent mixups; inspection results must be documented.
extra.baseline_failure_note: Describes documenting procedures for labelling integrity in general terms, cited to 820.10. 820.45(c)'s requirements - labelling and packaging operations established and maintained to prevent mixups, inspection before use against the medical device file, and documentation of inspection results under Clause 4.2.5 - are absent.

question: A firm wants to rely on a supplier certificate of analysis instead of testing a component for identity. Is that allowed?

context.heading: What must you do to determine whether specifications are met?

context.text:
(a) (a) You must visually examine each immediate container or grouping of immediate containers in a shipment that you receive for appropriate content label, container damage, or broken seals to determine whether the container condition may have resulted in contamination or deterioration of the components;
(b) (b) You must visually examine the supplier's invoice, guarantee, or certification in a shipment you receive to ensure the components are consistent with your purchase order;
context.heading: What requirements apply to components of dietary supplements?

answer:
It depends which specification you mean, and for the identity of a dietary ingredient the answer is no.

Identity of a dietary ingredient. You must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify the identity of any component that is a dietary ingredient, unless you petition the agency under 21 CFR 111.75(a)(1)(ii) and the agency exempts you (111.75(a)(1)(i)). A supplier certificate of analysis does not discharge this; the only route to relying on something else is a petition under 21 CFR 10.30 setting out the scientific rationale with supporting data for the proposed alternative testing (111.75(a)(1)(ii)).

Other component specifications. For components other than the identity of a dietary ingredient, you may rely on a certificate of analysis from the supplier, but only on conditions (111.75(a)(2)(ii)): you must first qualify the supplier by establishing the reliability of its certificate through confirmation of the results of the supplier's tests or examinations (A); the certificate must include a description of the test or examination methods used, the limits of the tests, and the actual results (B); and you must periodically re-confirm the supplier's certificate (D).

What you must do in any event. You must visually examine each immediate container or grouping of containers in a shipment for appropriate content label, container damage or broken seals, to determine whether the container condition may have resulted in contamination or deterioration (111.155(a)); and visually examine the supplier's invoice, guarantee or certification to ensure the components are consistent with your purchase order (111.155(b)).

question: If a requirement of ISO 13485 conflicts with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or another FDA regulation, which one governs?

context.text:

The requirements in this part govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use. The requirements in this part are intended to assure that finished devices will be safe and effective and otherwise in compliance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and that the use of other terminology, such as “safety and performance,” in this part does not change this statutory standard or the requirements of this part. Any manufacturers engaged in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, or servicing of a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system that is appropriate for its specific device(s). Manufacturers subject to this part include, but are not limited to, manufacturers that perform the functions of contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking, or specification development, as well as initial distributors of foreign entities that perform these functions. If a manufacturer engages in only some operations subject to the requirements in this part, and not in others, that manufacturer need only comply with those requirements applicable to the operations in which it is engaged.
(a)(2) (2) Components or parts. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, but such manufacturers are encouraged to consider provisions of this regulation as appropriate.
(b) (b) Conflicts with other requirements under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The QMSR for devices in this part supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise. To the extent that any applicable requirements in this part conflict with requirements in other parts of this chapter, the requirements specifically applicable to the device in question shall supersede the more generally applicable requirements. Moreover, to the extent that any clauses of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) conflict with any provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations will control.
(d) (d) Exemptions or variances.
context.heading: Scope.

context.text:
(a) (a) Document. Document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable requirements of this part; and
(b) (b) Applicable regulatory requirements. Comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in this title, including, but not limited to the following, to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 Clause:
context.heading: Requirements for a quality management system.

answer:
The Act and the applicable FDA regulations govern, not the standard.

21 CFR 820.1(b) sets out the order of precedence. The QMSR in Part 820 supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise. To the extent that any applicable requirements in Part 820 conflict with requirements in other parts of the chapter, the requirements specifically applicable to the device in question supersede the more generally applicable ones. And, to the extent that any clauses of ISO 13485 - incorporated by reference at 820.7 - conflict with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or with FDA regulations, the Act and those regulations prevail.

So incorporation by reference does not give the standard priority over US law. ISO 13485 is binding because 820.10(a) requires a documented quality management system complying with its applicable requirements, but where its text and a statutory or regulatory requirement cannot both be satisfied, the statutory or regulatory requirement is the one to follow.

The practical consequence is that the standard cannot be read as relaxing anything the Act or a Title 21 regulation requires, and 820.10(b) reinforces this by expressly routing certain clauses to the other Title 21 parts that govern them.

question: In plain English, why must a device manufacturer investigate a complaint, and what requires it?

context.heading: Control of records.

answer:
Because the regulation requires it, and the requirement is about keeping a record of the thinking as much as the outcome.

In plain terms: when someone complains that a device, its labeling or its packaging may not have met its specifications, the manufacturer has to look into it and write down what it found. That is how a pattern of failures becomes visible before it harms someone, and how FDA can see that the manufacturer noticed.

What requires it: 21 CFR 820.35(a). In addition to Clause 8.2.2 in ISO 13485, Complaint Handling - incorporated by reference at 820.7 - the manufacturer must maintain records of the review, evaluation and investigation of any complaint involving the possible failure of a device, labeling or packaging to meet any of its specifications. The record must include the name of the device, the date the complaint was received, any UDI or UPC and other device identification, the complainant's name, address and phone number, the nature and details of the complaint, any correction or corrective action taken, and any reply to the complainant (820.35(a)(1) through (7)).

So the duty to investigate comes from the incorporated standard's complaint handling clause; 820.35(a) is the Part 820 provision that makes the record of that investigation, and its contents, mandatory.

(c) (c) Labeling on or within the package from which the device is to be dispensed bears information for use, including indications, effects, routes, methods, and frequency and duration of administration, and any relevant hazards, contraindications, side effects, and precautions under which practitioners licensed by law to administer the device can use the device safely and for the purpose for which it is intended, including all purposes for which it is advertised or represented: Provided, however, That such information may be omitted from the dispensing package if, but only if, the article is a device for which directions, hazards, warnings, and other information are commonly known to practitioners licensed by law to use the device. (d) (d) Any labeling, as defined in section 201(m) of the act, whether or not it is on or within a package from which the device is to be dispensed, distributed by or on behalf of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor of the device, that furnishes or purports to furnish information for use of the device contains adequate information for such use, including indications, effects, routes, methods, and frequency and duration of administration and any relevant hazards, contraindications, side effects, and precautions, under which practitioners licensed by law to employ the device can use the device safely and for the purposes for which it is intended, including all purposes for which it is advertised or represented. This information will not be required on so-called reminder—piece labeling which calls attention to the name of the device but does not include indications or other use information.

answer:
How the exemption works. A device which, because of any potentiality for harmful effect, the method of its use, or the collateral measures necessary to its use, is not safe except under the supervision of a licensed practitioner - and for which adequate directions for lay use cannot be written - is exempt from the adequate directions for use requirement, provided the conditions of 21 CFR 801.109 are met.

The conditions. The device must be sold only to, or on the prescription or other order of, such a practitioner for use in the course of his professional practice (801.109(a)(2)). Its label must bear the symbol statement "Rx only" or "℞ only", or the statement "Caution: Federal law restricts this device to sale by or on the order of a ___", the blank filled with "physician", "dentist", "veterinarian" or the descriptive designation of the practitioner licensed to use or order the device (801.109(b)(1)).

Labeling. Labeling on or within the package from which the device is dispensed must bear information for use, including indications, effects, routes, methods, and frequency and duration of administration, and any relevant hazards, contraindications, side effects and precautions under which practitioners can use the device safely (801.109(c)).

Advertising and other labeling. Any labeling as defined in section 201(m) of the Act, whether or not on or within the package, distributed by or on behalf of the manufacturer, packer or distributor and furnishing information for use of the device, must meet the conditions 801.109(d) sets out. question: When may an institutional review board use expedited review procedures?

context.text:
(a) (a) The Food and Drug Administration has established, and published in the Federal Register, a list of categories of research that may be reviewed by the IRB through an expedited review procedure. The list will be amended, as appropriate, through periodic republication in the Federal Register.
(b) (b) An IRB may use the expedited review procedure to review either or both of the following:
(b)(1) (1) Some or all of the research appearing on the list and found by the reviewer(s) to involve no more than minimal risk, (2) minor changes in previously approved research during the period (of 1 year or less) for which approval is authorized. Under an expedited review procedure, the review may be carried out by the IRB chairperson or by one or more experienced reviewers designated by the IRB chairperson from among the members of the IRB. In reviewing the research, the reviewers may exercise all of the authorities of the IRB except that the reviewers may not disapprove the research. A research activity may be disapproved only after review in accordance with the nonexpedited review procedure set forth in § 56.108(c).
(c) (c) Each IRB which uses an expedited review procedure shall adopt a method for keeping all members advised of research proposals which have been approved under the procedure.
(d) (d) The Food and Drug Administration may restrict, suspend, or terminate an institution's or IRB's use of the expedited review procedure when necessary to protect the rights or welfare of subjects.
context.heading: Expedited review procedures for certain kinds of research involving no more than minimal risk, and for minor changes in approved research.

answer:
An IRB may use the expedited review procedure for either or both of two things (21 CFR 56.110(b)): some or all of the research appearing on the list FDA has established and published in the Federal Register, where the reviewer finds it involves no more than minimal risk (56.110(b)(1)); and minor changes in previously approved research during the period, of 1 year or less, for which approval is authorized.

Who may conduct it. Under the expedited procedure the review may be carried out by the IRB chairperson, or by one or more experienced reviewers designated by the chairperson from among the members of the IRB (56.110(b)).

Where the list comes from. FDA has established and published in the Federal Register a list of categories of research that may be reviewed through an expedited procedure, amended as appropriate by periodic republication (56.110(a)). So the first limb is not an open judgement about risk - the research has to fall within a published category and be found to involve no more than minimal risk.

Two controls on the procedure. Each IRB using it must adopt a method for keeping all members advised of research proposals approved under it (56.110(c)); and FDA may restrict, suspend or terminate an institution's or IRB's use of the procedure when necessary to protect the rights or welfare of subjects (56.110(d)).

(a)(2) (2) Components or parts. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, but such manufacturers are encouraged to consider provisions of this regulation as appropriate.

No to both.

No certification requirement. 21 CFR 820.10(a) requires a manufacturer subject to the part as described by 820.1(a) to document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, and the other applicable requirements of the part. question: What is the difference between the master production record and the batch production record?

context.heading: Master production and control records.
Batch production and control records.

answer:
The master record is the template; the batch record is the executed copy with evidence of what was actually done.

Master production and control records (21 CFR 211.186). To assure uniformity from batch to batch, master production and control records for each drug product, including each batch size, must be prepared, dated and signed - full signature, handwritten - by one person and independently checked, dated and signed by a second person (211.186(a)). They must include the name and strength of the product and a description of the dosage form; the name and weight or measure of each active ingredient per dosage unit or per unit of weight or measure, with a statement of the total weight or measure of any dosage unit; and a complete list of components designated by names or codes sufficiently specific to indicate any special quality characteristic (211.186(b)).

Batch production and control records (211.188). These must be prepared for each batch of drug product produced and must include complete information relating to the production and control of that batch. They must include an accurate reproduction of the appropriate master production or control record, checked for accuracy, dated and signed (211.188(a)); and documentation that each significant step in the manufacture, processing, packing or holding of the batch was accomplished, including the dates and the specific identification of each batch of component or in-process material used (211.188(b)).

So the distinguishing features are the two-person independent check on the master record, and the requirement that the batch record reproduce that master accurately and then evidence the actual execution of each significant step.

extra.key_elements: Master record content and independent verification; batch record as reproduction of the master with actual execution documentation.

Manufacturers of class II, class III, and those class I devices listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. The class I devices are as follows:
(c)(1) (1) Devices automated with computer software; and
(c)(2) (2) The devices listed in the following table:
(d) (d) Devices that support or sustain life. Manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements in this part, as appropriate.

answer:
Part 820 extends it by applying the standard's implantable-device traceability clause to a class of devices the standard would not itself reach.

21 CFR 820.10(d) provides that manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with the instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements.

So the trigger in the regulation is functional rather than anatomical. The standard's clause is written for implantable devices; 820.10(d) carries it across to life-supporting and life-sustaining devices on the basis of the consequence of failure, whether or not the device is implanted.

That sits alongside the general traceability cross-reference, which works differently: for Clause 7.5.9.1, Traceability - General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of Part 821, if applicable (820.10(b)(2)). One provision routes general traceability out to Part 821; the other extends the standard's own implantable-device clause to a wider set of devices.

question: What is the difference between a recall, a market withdrawal, and a stock recovery?

context.text:
(a) (a) Agency means the Food and Drug Administration.
(b) (b) Citation or cite means a document and any attachments thereto that provide notice to a person against whom criminal prosecution is contemplated of the opportunity to present views to the agency regarding an alleged violation.
(f) (f) Product means an article subject to the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration, including any food, drug, and device intended for human or animal use, any cosmetic and biologic intended for human use, any tobacco product intended for human use, and any item subject to a quarantine regulation under part 1240 of this chapter. Product does not include an electronic product that emits radiation and is subject to parts 1003 and 1004 of this chapter.
(g) (g) Recall means a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that the Food and Drug Administration considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action, e.g., seizure. Recall does not include a market withdrawal or a stock recovery.
(i) (i) Recalling firm means the firm that initiates a recall or, in the case of a Food and Drug Administration-requested recall, the firm that has primary responsibility for the manufacture and marketing of the product to be recalled.
(j) (j) Market withdrawal means a firm's removal or correction of a distributed product which involves a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action by the Food and Drug Administration or which involves no violation, e.g., normal stock rotation practices, routine equipment adjustments and repairs, etc.
(k) (k) Stock recovery means a firm's removal or correction of a product that has not been marketed or that has not left the direct control of the firm, i.e., the product is located on premises owned by, or under the control of, the firm and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use.
(l) (l) Recall strategy means a planned specific course of action to be taken in conducting a specific recall, which addresses the depth of recall, need for public warnings, and extent of effectiveness checks for the recall.
(m) (m) Recall classification means the numerical designation, i.e., I, II, or III, assigned by the Food and Drug Administration to a particular product recall to indicate the relative degree of health hazard presented by the product being recalled.
(m)(1) (1) Class I is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.
(m)(2) (2) Class II is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.
(m)(3) (3) Class III is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product is not likely to cause adverse health consequences.
context.heading: Definitions.

answer:
All three are defined in 21 CFR 7.3, and the distinction turns on two things: whether the product was marketed, and whether the violation would attract legal action.

Recall (7.3(g)) means a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that FDA considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action, for example seizure. The definition expressly excludes a market withdrawal and a stock recovery.

Market withdrawal (7.3(j)) means a firm's removal or correction of a distributed product which involves a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action by FDA, or which involves no violation at all - for example normal stock rotation practices or routine equipment adjustments and repairs. So the product has been distributed, but the defect is not one FDA would act on.

Stock recovery (7.3(k)) means a firm's removal or correction of a product that has not been marketed or that has not left the direct control of the firm - the product is on premises owned by or under the control of the firm and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use. So the product never reached the market.

The practical consequence is that only a recall carries the Part 7 machinery: a recall receives a classification of I, II or III reflecting the relative degree of health hazard (7.3(m)), and a recall strategy addressing depth of recall, the need for public warnings and the extent of effectiveness checks (7.3(l)). A market withdrawal and a stock recovery do not.

question: Under FSVP, how often must an importer re-verify a foreign supplier — every six months?

context.text:
(c) (c) Reevaluation of a foreign supplier's performance and the risk posed by a food.
(c)(1) (1) Except as specified in paragraph (d) of this section, you must promptly reevaluate the concerns associated with the factors in paragraph (a)(1) of this section when you become aware of new information about these factors, and the reevaluation must be documented. If you determine that the concerns associated with importing a food from a foreign supplier have changed, you must promptly determine (and document) whether it is appropriate to continue to import the food from the foreign supplier and whether the supplier verification activities conducted under § 1.506 or § 1.511(c) need to be changed.
(c)(2) (2) If at the end of any 3-year period you have not reevaluated the concerns associated with the factors in paragraph (a)(1) of this section in accordance with paragraph (c)(1) of this section, you must reevaluate those concerns and take other appropriate actions, if necessary, in accordance with paragraph (c)(1). You must document your reevaluation and any subsequent actions you take in accordance with paragraph (c)(1).
context.heading: What evaluation for foreign supplier approval and verification must I conduct?

context.text:
(d) (d) Determination of appropriate foreign supplier verification activities—
(d)(1)(i) (1)(i) General. Except as provided in paragraphs (d)(2) and (3) of this section, before importing a food from a foreign supplier, you must determine and document which verification activity or activities listed in paragraphs (d)(1)(ii)(A) through (D) of this section, as well as the frequency with which the activity or activities must be conducted, are needed to provide adequate assurances that the food you obtain from the foreign supplier is produced in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section. Verification activities must address the entity or entities that are significantly minimizing or preventing the hazards or verifying that the hazards have been significantly minimized or prevented (e.g., when an entity other than the grower of produce subject to part 112 of this chapter harvests or packs the produce and significantly minimizes or prevents the hazard or verifies that the hazard has been significantly minimized or prevented, or when the foreign supplier's raw material supplier significantly minimizes or prevents a hazard). The determination of appropriate supplier verification activities must be based on the evaluation of the food and foreign supplier conducted under § 1.505.
(d)(2) (2) Verification activities for certain serious hazards. When a hazard in a food will be controlled by the foreign supplier and is one for which there is a reasonable probability that exposure to the hazard will result in serious adverse health consequences or death to humans or animals, you must conduct or obtain documentation of an onsite audit of the foreign supplier before initially importing the food and at least annually thereafter, unless you make an adequate written determination that, instead of such initial and annual onsite auditing, other supplier verification activities listed in paragraph (d)(1)(ii) of this section and/or less frequent onsite auditing are appropriate to provide adequate assurances that the foreign supplier is producing the food in accordance with paragraph (c) of this section, based on the determination made under § 1.505.
context.heading: What foreign supplier verification and related activities must I conduct?

answer:
No, there is no six-month re-verification interval under FSVP. The premise is wrong, and two different requirements are being conflated.

Reevaluation of the supplier and the food. You must promptly reevaluate the concerns associated with the approval factors when you become aware of new information about them, and document the reevaluation; if the concerns have changed you must promptly determine whether to continue importing and what verification activities are appropriate (21 CFR 1.505(c)(1)). So the outer limit is 3 years, not 6 months, and an event-driven reevaluation can fall due at any time.

Frequency of verification activities. This is risk-based, not fixed: before importing, you must determine and document which verification activities, and the frequency with which they must be conducted, are needed to provide adequate assurances (1.506(d)(1)(i)). Where a hazard will be controlled by the foreign supplier and there is a reasonable probability that exposure to it would result in serious adverse health consequences or death, an onsite audit of the supplier is required before initially importing (1.506(d)(2)).

question: What are the record retention requirements?

context.heading: record retention periods differ by part: a sample of retention provisions across Title 21
context.source_key: absence:record retention periods differ by part: a sample of retention provisions across Title 21

answer:
Which part applies? Record retention periods in Title 21 differ by sector, and answering from one part would give you a figure that may be wrong for your product.

To take the examples in front of me: Part 117, for human food, sets its retention requirements at 117.315, including a longer period for records relating to the general adequacy of equipment or processes. Part 111 ties retention for dietary supplement records to the shelf life date where shelf life dating is used, and otherwise to the date of distribution of the last batch. Part 211 ties drug product record retention to the expiration date. Parts 803 and 806, for device reporting and for corrections and removals, use a period measured from the event or from the expected life of the device. Part 606, for blood and blood components, sets a substantially longer period for individual product records.

Tell me the product and the records in question - manufacturing, complaint, distribution or reporting records - and I will give you the governing retention provision and its exact period.

question: Who must establish and maintain records under the records access requirements, and what must those records contain?

context.text:
(a) (a) Persons who manufacture, process, pack, transport, distribute, receive, hold, or import food in the United States are subject to the regulations in this subpart, unless you qualify for one of the exclusions in § 1.327. If you conduct more than one type of activity at a location, you are required to keep records with respect to those activities covered by this subpart, but are not required by this subpart to keep records with respect to activities that fall within one of the exclusions in § 1.327.

context.heading: Who is subject to this subpart?
What information must nontransporters establish and maintain to identify the nontransporter and transporter immediate previous sources of food?

answer:
Who is subject. Persons who manufacture, process, pack, transport, distribute, receive, hold or import food in the United States are subject to subpart J, unless they qualify for one of the exclusions in 21 CFR 1.327; a person conducting more than one type of activity at a location is required to keep records for each activity (1.326(a)). The obligation applies whether or not the food is being offered for or enters interstate commerce (1.326(b)).

Records of the immediate previous source (1.337(a)). A nontransporter must establish and maintain, for all food it receives: the name, address and telephone number and, if available, the fax number and email address of the nontransporter immediate previous source, domestic or foreign; an adequate description of the type of food, including brand name and specific variety; the date received; for persons who manufacture, process or pack food, the lot or code number or other identifier to the extent it exists; the quantity and how the food is packaged; and the same contact details for the transporter that brought the food.

Records of the immediate subsequent recipient (1.345(a)). The same set is required for food released: the recipient's contact details, an adequate description of the food including brand name and specific variety, the date released, the lot or code number where applicable, the quantity and packaging, and the contact details of the transporter that took the food. The records must also include information reasonably available to identify the specific source of each ingredient used to make every lot of finished product (1.345(b)).

The "adequate description" standard is specific: brand x cheddar cheese, not just cheese; romaine lettuce, not just lettuce.

question: What current good manufacturing practice requirements apply to the manufacturing, processing, packing, and holding of animal food?

context.heading: Personnel.

context.text:
(a) (a) Human food by-products held for distribution as animal food must be held under conditions that will protect against contamination, including the following:
(a)(1) (1) Containers and equipment used to convey or hold human food by-products for use as animal food before distribution must be designed, constructed of appropriate material, cleaned as necessary, and maintained to protect against the contamination of human food by-products for use as animal food;
(a)(2) (2) Human food by-products for use as animal food held for distribution must be held in a way to protect against contamination from sources such as trash; and
(a)(3) (3) During holding, human food by-products for use as animal food must be accurately identified.
(b) (b) Labeling that identifies the product by the common or usual name must be affixed to or accompany the human food by-products for use as animal food when distributed.
(c) (c) Shipping containers (e.g., totes, drums, and tubs) and bulk vehicles used to distribute human food by-products for use as animal food must be examined prior to use to protect against the contamination of animal food from the container or vehicle when the facility is responsible for transporting the human food by-products for use as animal food itself or arranges with a third party to transport the human food by-products for use as animal food.
context.heading: Holding and distribution of human food by-products for use as animal food.

answer:
Personnel (21 CFR 507.14). The management of the establishment must take reasonable measures and precautions to ensure that all persons working in direct contact with animal food, animal food-contact surfaces and animal food-packaging materials conform to hygienic practices and maintain cleanliness (507.14(a)). The methods include maintaining adequate personal cleanliness; washing hands thoroughly in an adequate hand-washing facility as necessary and appropriate to protect against contamination; removing or securing jewelry and other objects that might fall into animal food, equipment or containers; and storing clothing and other personal belongings away from areas where animal food is exposed or equipment and utensils are cleaned (507.14(b)).

Holding and distribution of human food by-products for use as animal food (507.28). By-products held for distribution as animal food must be held under conditions protecting against contamination: containers and equipment used to convey or hold them must be designed, constructed of appropriate material, cleaned as necessary and maintained so as to protect against contamination; the by-products must be held so as to protect against contamination from sources such as trash; and during holding they must be accurately identified (507.28(a)). Labeling identifying the product by its common or usual name must be affixed to or accompany the by-products when distributed (507.28(b)), and shipping containers such as totes, drums and tubs, and bulk vehicles used to distribute them, must be examined prior to use to protect against contamination (507.28(c)).

The subpart also carries requirements for plant and grounds, sanitation, water supply and plumbing, equipment and utensils, and processes and controls, each in its own section of subpart B.

extra.key_elements: Personnel, plant and grounds, sanitation, water supply and plumbing, equipment and utensils, processes and controls, warehousing and distribution, and holding and distribution of human food by-products.

question: What are the requirements for labeling issuance and control?

context.text:
(a) (a) There shall be written procedures describing in sufficient detail the receipt, identification, storage, handling, sampling, examination, and/or testing of labeling and packaging materials; such written procedures shall be followed. Labeling and packaging materials shall be representatively sampled, and examined or tested upon receipt and before use in packaging or labeling of a drug product.
(c) (c) Records shall be maintained for each shipment received of each different labeling and packaging material indicating receipt, examination or testing, and whether accepted or rejected.
(d) (d) Labels and other labeling materials for each different drug product, strength, dosage form, or quantity of contents shall be stored separately with suitable identification. Access to the storage area shall be limited to authorized personnel.
(e) (e) Obsolete and outdated labels, labeling, and other packaging materials shall be destroyed.
(f) (f) Use of gang-printed labeling for different drug products, or different strengths or net contents of the same drug product, is prohibited unless the labeling from gang-printed sheets is adequately differentiated by size, shape, or color.
(g) (g) If cut labeling is used for immediate container labels, individual unit cartons, or multiunit cartons containing immediate containers that are not packaged in individual unit cartons, packaging and labeling operations shall include one of the following special control procedures:
(g)(2) (2) Use of appropriate electronic or electromechanical equipment to conduct a 100-percent examination for correct labeling during or after completion of finishing operations; or
context.heading: Materials examination and usage criteria.

context.text:
(a) (a) Strict control shall be exercised over labeling issued for use in drug product labeling operations.
(b) (b) Labeling materials issued for a batch shall be carefully examined for identity and conformity to the labeling specified in the master or batch production records.
(c) (c) Procedures shall be used to reconcile the quantities of labeling issued, used, and returned, and shall require evaluation of discrepancies found between the quantity of drug product finished and the quantity of labeling issued when such discrepancies are outside narrow preset limits based on historical operating data. Such discrepancies shall be investigated in accordance with § 211.192. Labeling reconciliation is waived for cut or roll labeling if a 100-percent examination for correct labeling is performed in accordance with § 211.122(g)(2).
(d) (d) All excess labeling bearing lot or control numbers shall be destroyed.
(e) (e) Returned labeling shall be maintained and stored in a manner to prevent mixups and provide proper identification.
(f) (f) Procedures shall be written describing in sufficient detail the control procedures employed for the issuance of labeling; such written procedures shall be followed.
context.heading: Labeling issuance.

answer:
Two sections work together.

Materials examination and control (21 CFR 211.122). There must be written procedures describing in sufficient detail the receipt, identification, storage, handling, sampling, examination and/or testing of labeling and packaging materials, and those procedures must be followed; the materials must be representatively sampled and examined or tested on receipt and before use (211.122(a)). Records must be maintained for each shipment received of each different labeling and packaging material, indicating receipt, examination or testing, and whether accepted or rejected (211.122(c)). Labels and other labeling for each different drug product, strength, dosage form or quantity of contents must be stored separately with suitable identification, with access limited to authorized personnel (211.122(d)), and obsolete and outdated labels and packaging materials must be destroyed (211.122(e)).

Gang printing (211.122(f)). The use of gang-printed labeling for different drug products, or different strengths or net contents of the same drug product, is prohibited unless the labeling from gang-printed sheets is adequately differentiated by size, shape or colour.

Cut labeling (211.122(g)). Where cut labeling is used for immediate container labels or unit or multiunit cartons, packaging and labeling operations must include one of the special control procedures the paragraph specifies - for example the use of appropriate electronic or electromechanical equipment to conduct a 100-percent examination for correct labeling during or after finishing operations (211.122(g)(2)).

Labeling issuance (211.125). Strict control must be exercised over labeling issued for use (211.125(a)); labeling issued for a batch must be carefully examined for identity and conformity to the labeling specified in the master or batch production records (211.125(b)); procedures must reconcile the quantities of labeling issued, used and returned, and must require evaluation of discrepancies outside narrow preset limits (211.125(c)); all excess labeling bearing lot or control numbers must be destroyed (211.125(d)); returned labeling must be maintained and stored so as to prevent mixups and provide proper identification (211.125(e)); and the control procedures for issuance must be written and followed (211.125(f)).

extra.key_elements: Written procedures for receipt, identification, storage, handling, sampling, examination; issuance and reconciliation of labels; gang printing restrictions.

question: What representative samples must be collected under Part 111, and what reserve sample requirements apply?

context.heading: What representative samples must you collect?
What are the requirements for reserve samples?

answer:
Representative samples (21 CFR 111.80). You must collect representative samples of: each unique lot of components, packaging and labels you use, to determine whether they meet the specifications established under 111.70(b) and (d) and, as applicable, 111.70(a) (111.80(a)); in-process materials for each manufactured batch, at the points, steps or stages specified in the master manufacturing record where control is necessary to ensure identity, purity, strength and composition (111.80(b)); a subset of finished batches of each dietary supplement you manufacture, identified through a sound statistical sampling plan - or otherwise every finished batch - before releasing for distribution (111.80(c)); each unique shipment, and each unique lot within each shipment, of product you receive for packaging or labeling as a dietary supplement for distribution (111.80(d)); and each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplements, to determine whether the packaging and labeling meet the specifications established under 111.70(g) (111.80(e)).

Reserve samples (111.83). You must collect and hold reserve samples of each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplements that you distribute (111.83(a)). They must be held using the same container-closure system in which the product is distributed, or one providing essentially the same protective characteristics (111.83(b)(1)); be identified with the batch, lot or control number (111.83(b)(2)); and be retained for 1 year past the shelf life date, if shelf life dating is used, or for 2 years from the date of distribution of the last batch associated with the reserve sample, for use in appropriate investigations (111.83(b)(3)).

question: What must the batch production record contain under Part 111?

context.heading: What must the batch record include?
What is the requirement to establish a batch production record?

answer:
21 CFR 111.260 sets out what the batch production record must include. It begins with identification: the batch, lot or control number of the finished batch of dietary supplement, and of each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplement from that finished batch (111.260(a)).

It must also record the identity of the equipment and processing lines used in producing the batch (111.260(b)); and the date and time of the maintenance, cleaning and sanitizing of that equipment and those processing lines, or a cross-reference to records such as individual equipment logs where that information is kept (111.260(c)).

The remaining paragraphs of the section carry the rest of the required content, including the identity and weight or measure of each component used, the dates of manufacture, the initials of the persons performing and of those verifying each controlled step, the results of any tests or examinations, and documentation of any deviation from the master manufacturing record.

The governing constraint on all of it is 111.255(c): the batch production record must accurately follow the appropriate master manufacturing record, and each step in the production of the batch must actually be performed.

question: What are the ventilation, air filtration, and air heating/cooling requirements under Part 211?

(c) (c) Air filtration systems, including prefilters and particulate matter air filters, shall be used when appropriate on air supplies to production areas. If air is recirculated to production areas, measures shall be taken to control recirculation of dust from production. answer:
21 CFR 211.46 sets four requirements.

Adequate ventilation shall be provided (211.46(a)).

Equipment for adequate control over air pressure, micro-organisms, dust, humidity and temperature shall be provided when appropriate for the manufacture, processing, packing or holding of a drug product (211.46(b)).

Air filtration systems, including prefilters and particulate matter air filters, shall be used when appropriate on air supplies to production areas. If air is recirculated to production areas, measures shall be taken to control recirculation of dust from production, and in areas where air contamination occurs during production there shall be adequate exhaust systems or other systems adequate to control contaminants (211.46(c)).

Air-handling systems for the manufacture, processing and packing of penicillin shall be completely separate from those for other drug products for human use (211.46(d)). That last requirement is absolute - it is not qualified by "when appropriate", unlike paragraphs (b) and (c).
